destination.title: A Doctor Reports Police Torture in 1982. The Letter Is Buried for 33 Years.

short59: Why does Chicago teach its eighth graders
about one police commander?
His name was Jon Burge.
For two decades
detectives under his command on Chicago's South
Side tortured confessions out of more than
one hundred Black men.
Survivors described a hand-cranked box with two wires. Electric shock. Suffocation. Mock executions. In 1982
a jail doctor demanded in writing
an investigation of the brutality.
The letter reached the top
and nothing happened. For decades
complaints fell on deaf ears.
By the time the truth was official
the statute of limitations had run out.
The torture could never be prosecuted.
So federal prosecutors charged the only crime left
lying about it under oath.
Four and a half years.
He kept his police pension until the
day he died.
Chicago passed America's first municipal reparations for police violence
and put this story in its schools
so the city can never say it didn't know.
Follow for the cases they don't teach you.
short66: In February of 1982
a doctor at the Cook County Jail
examined a new prisoner and found injuries
he could not explain away.
So the doctor did what doctors are
supposed to do.
He wrote a letter to the superintendent
of the Chicago Police Department
describing the injuries demanding his words
a thorough investigation.
That letter went up the chain of command
landed on the desk of one of
the most powerful men in Illinois
and died there. No answer. No investigation. Nothing.
For five weeks
a federal courtroom heard everything the statute
of limitations had buried. Melvin Jones.
The medical records. The letter.
He was never charged with torture
only with lying about it.
The full case is on the channel.
Follow for the cases they don't teach you.

shorts.angle: Illinois gave prosecutors three years to charge these crimes, so the clock on every provable case had already run out before the state agreed the torture was real.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: If every provable crime had expired, what was the one thing left that a federal jury could still convict him of?

lines.text: Two special prosecutors spent four years and about seven million dollars investigating Chicago police torture. Charges filed against anyone: none.
source_lines: They worked for four years. They spent about seven million dollars.

lines.text: Illinois gave prosecutors three years to bring charges for aggravated battery or official misconduct. Three years from the moment the crank turned.
source_lines: aggravated battery, official misconduct — Illinois law gave prosecutors three years.
Three years from the moment the crank turned to the last day charges could be filed.

lines.text: Anthony Holmes was tortured in 1973. That clock died in 1976. Andrew Wilson, February 1982; that clock died in February 1985.
source_lines: Anthony Holmes, 1973: the clock died in 1976. Andrew Wilson, February 1982: the clock died in February 1985

lines.text: Every victim of the eighties expired by the early nineties, before the police department's own report on Area 2 ever saw daylight.
source_lines: Every victim of the eighties: expired by the early nineties, before the Goldston report ever saw daylight.

lines.text: The special prosecutors examined one hundred and forty-eight torture claims and believed torture had occurred in roughly half of them.
source_lines: They examined one hundred and forty-eight claims of torture.
They believed torture had occurred in roughly half the cases they examined.

lines.text: In three cases they found proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Enough evidence to convict in any courtroom in America.
source_lines: In three of them — Andrew Wilson's among them — they found proof beyond a reasonable doubt: enough evidence, right now, to convict Jon Burge and his men in any courtroom in America.

lines.text: They had built a perfect case for a trial that could never legally begin. Every provable crime was decades past its clock.
source_lines: The special prosecutors had built a perfect case for a trial that could never legally begin.
Every provable crime was decades past its three-year clock.

lines.text: The state had finally, officially, expensively believed the victims. Its belief was worth nothing, because it arrived after the deadline.
source_lines: The state of Illinois had finally, officially, expensively believed the victims — and its belief was worth nothing.

shorts.loop_join: L8 ends on a belief that arrived after the deadline, which is exactly why L1's four-year, seven-million-dollar investigation finishes with no charges at all.
